title: 2 Digit by 1 Digit Multiplication for Grade 3 (Column Method + Free Quiz)
meta_title: 2 Digit by 1 Digit Multiplication Grade 3 + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach 2 digit by 1 digit multiplication in Grade 3 the column way, with carrying explained step by step, plus a free quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: 34 × 6 trips up half a Grade 3 class — not because of the tables, but because of the carry. Here is the column method taught the way it finally sticks, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 34 × 6 on the board in a Grade 3 class and watch what happens. A few children multiply 6 by the 4, get 24, and write all of it under the line — then multiply 6 by the 3 and tack that on the front. Out comes an answer like 2418. The tables were perfect; the method fell apart at the carry. That single stumble is what 2 digit by 1 digit multiplication in Grade 3 is really about, and it is fixable in a week.

This guide assumes your child already knows the times tables from 1 to 10. If those are still shaky, sort that first — a separate skill, a separate blog. Here we do one job: turn known tables into a reliable written method for numbers like 34 × 6, 52 × 4 and 19 × 7, carrying and all.

Start with the expanded way, not the shortcut

Before any child writes numbers in neat columns, they should see why the method works. Split the two-digit number into tens and ones. For 34 × 6, that is 30 + 4.

Now multiply each part by 6 and add the two results. This is the partial-products idea, and it is the honest picture of what multiplication is doing:

  • 4 × 6 = 24 (the ones)
  • 30 × 6 = 180 (the tens)
  • 24 + 180 = 204

Spend two or three days here. Let your child write out both partial products every single time. It feels slow, and that is the point — they are building the mental model that the compact method will later hide. When a child understands that the ‘carry’ is really the extra tens from that 24, the shortcut stops being magic and starts being sense.

The column method, step by step

Once partial products are comfortable, stack the numbers with the ones lined up and the single digit underneath. Then work right to left.

A worked example: 34 × 6

Multiply the ones first. 4 × 6 = 24. That is 2 tens and 4 ones, so write the 4 under the ones column and carry the 2 above the tens column — a small 2, lightly, so it does not get muddled with the answer.

Now multiply the tens. 3 × 6 = 18. Add the carried 2: 18 + 2 = 20. Write 20 to the left of the 4. The answer reads 204. Notice it matches the expanded working exactly — that is the proof the shortcut is trustworthy.

The one instruction I repeat most: multiply first, then add the carry. Children who add the carry before multiplying (3 + 2, then × 6) get it wrong every time. Multiply, then add. Say it out loud together.

StepExpanded wayColumn way
Ones4 × 6 = 24Write 4, carry 2
Tens30 × 6 = 1803 × 6 = 18, +2 = 20
Combine24 + 180 = 204Answer: 204

Estimate first to catch the big mistakes

Here is the habit that separates a careful child from a lucky one: estimate before you calculate. Round the two-digit number to the nearest ten and multiply in your head. For 34 × 6, round 34 to 30 (or 40) and think ‘about 180 to 240.’ So an answer of 204 looks right, and that earlier answer of 2418 is instantly, obviously absurd.

This one-second check catches the classic place-value blunders that carrying causes. I ask children to whisper the estimate before they pick up the pencil. It costs nothing and saves marks in every test they will ever sit.

Common carrying mistakes — and the fix

Almost every error in 2 digit by 1 digit multiplication comes from a small handful of slips. Knowing them in advance means you can name the mistake the moment it appears, which is far more useful than a red cross.

  • Forgetting to add the carry. The child multiplies the tens correctly but leaves out the small carried digit. Fix: cross the carry out once it is used, so it is clearly ‘spent.’
  • Adding the carry before multiplying. For 34 × 6 they do 3 + 2 = 5, then 5 × 6. Fix: chant ‘times first, then plus.’
  • Writing the whole two-digit product in the ones column. Getting 24 and writing both digits under the ones. Fix: go back to the ten-frame idea — 24 is 2 tens and 4 ones, and tens cannot live in the ones column.
  • Misaligned columns. Sloppy stacking sends digits into the wrong place. Fix: squared paper, one digit per box.

A realistic week of practice

Short and daily wins. Two days on expanded partial products, then three days moving to the column method, with an estimate whispered before each sum. Mix in a few word problems — ‘18 sweets in each of 7 boxes’ — so the child sees where this actually shows up. Ten focused minutes beats a marathon on Sunday, and the estimate habit should ride along on every single question until it becomes automatic.

One honest trade-off: do not rush a child off the expanded method too soon just because the column way looks tidier. The tidy method is only safe once the reasoning underneath it is solid. Push too early and you get fast, confident, wrong answers.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

The eight-question quiz below covers exactly what we did here — carrying, estimating, and spotting the wrong answer. Let your child work each one, then read the explanations together for anything missed. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 3 2-Digit × 1-Digit Multiplication Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the column method, carrying and estimating. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 multiplication of a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number

questions.explanation: Ones: 3 × 3 = 9, write 9, no carry. Tens: 2 × 3 = 6. The answer is 69.
Ones: 4 × 6 = 24, write 4 carry 2. Tens: 3 × 6 = 18, plus the carried 2 is 20. The answer is 204.

questions.q: In 47 × 5, you multiply the ones: 7 × 5 = 35. Which digit do you carry?
questions.explanation: 35 is 3 tens and 5 ones. Write the 5, carry the 3 to the tens column.

questions.q: Estimate 38 × 4 by rounding 38 to 40. About how big is the answer?
questions.explanation: 40 × 4 = 160, so the real answer (152) should be near 160. This catches wild mistakes.
Ones: 2 × 4 = 8, write 8, no carry. Tens: 5 × 4 = 20. The answer is 208.
Ones: 9 × 7 = 63, write 3 carry 6. Tens: 1 × 7 = 7, plus 6 is 13. The answer is 133.
Ones: 6 × 3 = 18, write 8 carry 1. Tens: 2 × 3 = 6, plus 1 is 7. The answer is 78.
Ones: 1 × 8 = 8, write 8, no carry. Tens: 7 × 8 = 56. The answer is 568.

faq.q: Should my child learn the column method or partial products first?
faq.a: Partial products first. Splitting 34 into 30 + 4 and multiplying each part shows why the method works. Once that is understood, the column shortcut with carrying makes sense instead of being memorised blindly.
When the ones digits multiply to more than 9, you get extra tens. For 4 × 6 = 24, the 2 is 2 tens that belong in the tens column — so you carry it over and add it after multiplying the tens.

faq.q: Why does my child add the carry before multiplying?
faq.a: It is the most common slip in Grade 3. The rule is fixed: multiply the tens digit first, then add the carried number. Saying ‘times first, then plus’ out loud on every question fixes it within a few days.

faq.q: How important is estimating the answer?
faq.a: Very. Rounding the two-digit number to the nearest ten and multiplying in your head gives a rough target. If the written answer is far from it, the child knows to check — usually a missed or misplaced carry.
